findings.headline: Cumulative inflationary pressures of £4.8M concentrated in early MTFS years
findings.detail: The MTFS forecasts inflationary pressures of £1,224k in 2026/27 alone, with cumulative inflation reaching £4,757k by 2029/30. Pressures listed include water rates, commissions, Awaabs Law compliance, and ICT pressures. The sharp front-loading (declining from £1,224k to £280k by 2030/31) suggests major step-change or one-time compliance costs in the early period.
findings.matters: Material inflationary pressures in early years could stress the HRA's ability to deliver the unidentified savings and maintain balance if not properly anticipated.
findings.quote: Inflationary Pressures in the MTFS shows £1,224k in 2026/27 and Cumm Inflation reaching £4,757k by 2029/30

findings.headline: HRA reserves declining 18% from £12.5M to £10.3M, driven by negative in-year balances usage
findings.detail: Closing reserve balances fall from £12,538k in 2027/28 to £10,289k in 2030/31. The decline reflects negative in-year uses of balances throughout: £697k (2027/28), £899k (2028/29), £749k (2030/31), showing the HRA is drawing on reserves to balance its budget. This reduces financial buffer for cost pressures or income shortfalls.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce capacity to absorb volatility; a lender would need to understand whether £10.3M represents adequate minimum reserves and what triggers further drawdown.
findings.figures: HRA Reserves: 2027/28 closing £12,538k, 2028/29 closing £11,840k, 2029/30 closing £11,038k, 2030/31 closing £10,289k. Decline of £2,249k (18%) over 4 years.
findings.quote: HRA Reserves and use of balances each year £'000 shows Closing Balance declining from £12,538k in 2027/28 to £10,289k in 2030/31

findings.headline: HRA Business Plan forecasts £14M higher debt than MTFS by 2030/31
findings.detail: The Business Plan shows total HRA debt reaching £353M by 2030/31, compared to £339M in the MTFS. This £14M divergence persists across earlier years too: 2027/28 Business Plan £314M vs MTFS £303M (£11M gap). The divergence suggests different capital spending or financing assumptions between the two plans, creating uncertainty about actual debt trajectory.
findings.matters: Material divergence between planning scenarios raises questions about debt assumptions, sustainability, and which plan better represents likely debt service obligations.
findings.figures: 2030/31: MTFS Loans £339M, HRA Bus. Plan Loans £353M gap £14M. Also 2027/28 MTFS £303M vs Business Plan £314M, and 2028/29 MTFS £318M vs Business Plan £327M.
findings.quote: HRA Debt Forecasts £'Million shows 2030/31 MTFS Loans £339M and HRA Bus. Plan Loans £353M

findings.headline: Unidentified savings gap of £2.6M by 2030/31 despite escalating savings targets
findings.detail: The MTFS forecasts savings targets rising from £1,679k to £3,579k, but has only identified £959k in each year 2027/28-2030/31. The gap widens from £720k in 2027/28 to £2,620k in 2030/31. The council's financial plan relies on delivering savings that have not yet been identified, creating material execution risk.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that the financial plan is deliverable; unidentified savings of £2.6M represents a substantial hole in the budget that the council has not yet explained.
findings.figures: 2030/31 Savings Targets £3,579k, Savings Target Identified £959k, gap £2,620k. Similar gaps: 2027/28 £720k, 2028/29 £1,720k, 2029/30 £2,220k.
findings.quote: Savings Target v identified and recommended for approval (£'000) shows 2030/31 Savings Targets £3,579k with Savings Target Identified only £959k

findings.headline: Compensation for use of a car park as a construction compound (Swingate JV) is ending in December 2026, removing a £200K annual income benefit starting 2027/28
findings.detail: The Swingate Joint Venture (Mace partnership for SG1 regeneration) has compensated the council for use of a car park as a construction compound. This agreement ends in December 2026, removing a temporary income stream. The MTFS shows £200K annual loss starting 2027/28. This loss reduces net income and reveals the underlying operational cost of supporting the regeneration programme.
findings.matters: The council is losing a temporary income stream that masked the true operational cost of regeneration. The underlying funding gap is now more visible and must be absorbed by balances or savings.
findings.figures: Compensation ends December 2026; annual income loss £200K from 2027/28 onwards.
findings.quote: Swingate JV compensated the Council for the use of the car park as a compound, this is due to end in December 2026.

findings.headline: Investment income is declining as cash balances fall; if external borrowing becomes necessary at 6.05%, it will cost an extra £20K per million borrowed compared to current internal rates
findings.detail: The council currently avoids external borrowing (PWLB) because investment returns exceed borrowing costs. Average cash balances are projected to decline from £24.8M (2026/27) to £18.7M by 2030/31, while investment rates fall from 4.25% to 2.0%. If balances fall below operational need, external borrowing at 6.05% will consume £20K per million borrowed in additional cost. The council has not borrowed for General Fund prudential borrowing to date, signalling reliance on cash.
findings.matters: Declining cash reserves and falling investment returns signal the council may shift from net cash-positive to net borrowing within the MTFS period. This structural funding change is material to a lender's assessment.
findings.figures: Average cash balances 2026/27 £24.8M at 4.25% → 2030/31 £18.7M at 2.0%; external borrowing cost 6.05% vs internal 4.25% = £20K per million borrowed.
findings.quote: If the General Fund needs to externally borrow, based on an average rate of lost investment income at 4.25% versus a borrowing rate currently of 6.05% would be an extra £20,000 per million externally borrowed.

findings.headline: A stock condition survey of council assets is due in October 2026; the council has budgeted £200K for repairs in each of 2026/27 and 2027/28 but the full extent of required works is unknown
findings.detail: A new Head of Property Services has commissioned a survey of non-housing assets for the first time in several years. Results are due October 2026. The MTFS includes £200K RCCO for each of 2026/27 and 2027/28 to fund works, but the CFO explicitly notes that 'it is likely that works will be required' and the full scope is uncertain. The CFO identifies this as a risk in section 5.3: 'Stock condition survey results may show a higher level of works required than available'.
findings.matters: Asset backlogs typically exceed budgeted remediation. The council has allocated a fixed amount against an unknown liability. If works exceed budget, this will draw on balances or reduce other spending.
findings.figures: Survey results due October 2026; budgeted RCCO £200K each year (2026/27–2027/28); full extent of required works unknown.
findings.quote: A Stock condition survey has been commissioned by the new Head of Property Services to understand the condition of the Councils non housing assets and was trailed in the Capital Strategy, with the previous survey being a number of years ago. It is likely that works will be required, (due October 2026).

findings.headline: The council's auditors are requiring a catch-up review back to 2021/22 to achieve a clean audit opinion, with £100K estimated cost for 2026/27 and 2027/28
findings.detail: The Statement of Accounts has not received a clean audit opinion in recent years (last clean opinion 2021/22). The auditors are implementing a 'build back programme' to reconcile five years of accounts to a clean baseline. This is estimated at £100K per year for 2026/27 and 2027/28 and signals prior control or accounting weaknesses that have taken years to surface.
findings.matters: Audit delays or qualifications signal weaknesses in financial control and governance. A lender assesses audit risk as a proxy for the council's ability to manage finances accurately. The backlog suggests prior-year errors or systems not fit for purpose.
findings.figures: Audit back programme £100K per annum (2026/27 and 2027/28); reconciliation required to 2021/22 clean opinion baseline.
findings.quote: The Council's Auditors will be setting out the build back programme to ensure a clean opinion on the Statement of Accounts by 2027/28. The work requires reconciling back to the last clean opinion set of accounts which is 2021/22 so this is likely to entail significantly more costs.

findings.headline: A £5.33M voluntary MRP repayment for LEP loans falls due in 2029/30, creating a cliff-edge cash call that will fall to the new unitary authority, not Stevenage
findings.detail: Stevenage holds Local Enterprise Partnership loans for SG1 site regeneration. The MTFS includes annual MRP of £131.4K with a voluntary MRP (VMRP) repayment of £5.33M in 2029/30 required by loan terms. The council's NNDR reserve is being used to fund this (£2.47M use across MTFS). The new unitary could defer and pay annual MRP instead if cash balances allow, but this choice rests with the successor authority, not Stevenage.
findings.matters: This creates a significant unplanned cash call in 2029/30 that will fall to the new unitary authority. The NNDR reserve is being depleted to cover it; reserves available to the council are constrained.
findings.figures: LEP MRP 2026/27 £848K, 2027/28–2028/29 £131K each year; VMRP 2029/30 £5.33M; NNDR reserve funding £2.47M total.
findings.quote: The Local Enterprise Partnership (LEP now Herts Futures) loans includes a voluntary MRP repayment in 2029/30 of £5.33Million as this coincides with the requirement to repay the remaining loans back to Herts Futures in 2029/30.

findings.headline: The council has identified only £67.5K of the £350K Balancing the Budget target for 2027/28, leaving £282.5K to find from fees, charges and unspecified 'star chamber' options
findings.detail: The Balancing the Budget savings target is much lower than the historic £18M delivered (2010/11–2026/27) due to Fair Funding. However, only £67.5K has been identified to date against a 2027/28 target of £350K. Options secured include tipping income rebudgeting (£42.8K), Citizens Advice renegotiation (£20.1K), procurement income (£4.6K) and commercial lease renewals (£13K). The CFO states that £260K remains to be found from fees and charges and 'star chamber' options, expressing confidence this will be delivered, but these are not yet secured.
findings.matters: Fair Funding masks an underlying savings requirement. If options fail to materialise, the council will draw on balances. The target extends beyond 2028/29 (LGR vesting), so the new unitary inherits this commitment.
findings.figures: 2027/28 target £350K; identified £67.5K; to find £282.5K; cumulative 2027/28–2030/31 target £1.2M.
findings.quote: The Balancing the Budget target of £1.2Million, be approved for the period 2027/28- 2030/31, as set out in section 4.10 of the report, (subject to decisions made after 2027/28 by the new Unitary Authority).

findings.headline: The council will cease to exist on 1 April 2028 when it merges into a new Central Hertfordshire unitary, creating transition costs and governance uncertainty through the end of the MTFS period
findings.detail: Stevenage will merge into a new unitary authority with shadow elections in May 2027 and vesting on 1 April 2028. The MTFS extends to 2030/31, beyond the council's dissolution. The council has allocated £500K (2026/27) and £650K (2027/28) to a central LGR programme board from an estimated total cost of £23M. The CFO recommends additional provision of £500K (2026/27) and £550K (2027/28), suggesting underfunding risk. Section 24 Direction restrictions will limit disposals over £100K and non-capital contracts over £100K without consent, reducing management flexibility.
findings.matters: A lender cannot assess post-2028 resilience because the borrower ceases to exist. Transition costs may exceed budgets and absorb reserves. The new authority's financial position and role are unknown.
findings.figures: Total LGR programme cost £23M (estimate); council contribution £1.15M budgeted (2026/27–2027/28) plus £1.05M recommended additional; vesting 1 April 2028.
findings.quote: Stevenage Borough Council administration will change from 2028/29 into a larger unitary Council... From April 2028, this means combining upper and lower tier functions into a single unitary Council in central Hertfordshire.

findings.headline: Business rates reset in 2026/27 eliminated the council's historic gains and left it at baseline with £7.4M in appeals outstanding, £1.9M on the 2017 list alone
findings.detail: The government reset business rates baselines in 2026/27 to 'eliminate historic NNDR gains', raising Stevenage's tariff by £3.3M (16.96%) but increasing only the retained baseline by 6.8%. The council now retains business rates at baseline with no growth. If all £7.4M in outstanding appeals succeed, retained NNDR could fall to £1.4M against the £3.6M baseline. The safety net provides 100% protection for 2026/27 but drops to 95% (2027/28) and 92.5% (2028/29), exposing the council to losses of £185K and £282K respectively.
findings.matters: The council has lost its historic NNDR flexibility and operates at baseline with tail risk from appeals and declining safety-net protection. Revenue risk is embedded across the MTFS.
findings.figures: Outstanding appeals £7.4M (£1.9M on 2017 list); tariff increase £3.3M (16.96%); baseline increase £3.61M (6.8%); safety net 100% (2026/27), 95% (2027/28), 92.5% (2028/29).
findings.quote: There are currently £7.4Million rating appeals outstanding with £1.9Million relating to the 2017 rating list. When the estimate was completed for 2026/27 no gains were projected and the retained business rates for Stevenage are at the baseline level.

findings.headline: Fair Funding reform has lifted the council's funding by £1.28M annually but ends in 2028/29 when the district dissolves into a new unitary authority
findings.detail: Core Spending Power rose 9.2% year-on-year from 2025/26 to 2026/27 (£1.28M increase), significantly outpacing England's 6.14% average. However, Fair Funding is a three-year settlement ending in 2028/29, coinciding exactly with the council's vesting into the new Central Hertfordshire unitary. Beyond then, only a 2% annual uplift is assumed, but the council will cease to exist and the new authority will inherit pressures from adult social care and children's services.
findings.matters: Lenders must distinguish one-off gains from sustainable income; this windfall ends precisely when the council restructures and inherits new statutory duties, creating a cliff-edge.
findings.figures: Core Spending Power 2025/26 £13.86M → 2026/27 £15.14M (9.2% increase); Fair Funding covers 2026/27–2028/29 only.
findings.quote: Fair Funding was implemented by the government in 2026/27, and local government resources were set out for a three-year period... The final year of Fair Funding spending period covers the first year of the new Hertfordshire unitaries.

findings.paper_title: 7 Annual Treasury Management Review Prudential Indicators 2025-26
findings.headline: All available cash buffers allocated to future spending; council acknowledges future reliance on external borrowing when rates are expected to remain elevated
findings.detail: The council's £52M investment balance is fully allocated (62% to capital schemes, 15% HRA reserves, 9% GF reserves, 14% statutory minimums). Treasury note: 'The policy of avoiding new borrowing by running down spare cash balances has served the Council well over the last few years. However, this has been kept under review to avoid incurring higher borrowing costs in the future when the Council may not be able to avoid new borrowing.' Bank rate expected to remain at 3.75% into 2026/27; long-dated rates expected to remain 'expensive'.
findings.matters: The council's strategy of internal borrowing (using reserves) to avoid external borrowing costs has run its course. Future capital delivery and HRA spending will require new external borrowing at rates the council describes as 'expensive' and expects to remain elevated. This creates both cost risk and refinancing risk.
findings.figures: Investment balance £51.865M (all allocated); cash inflow to HRA £12M to replenish internal borrowing; expected Bank Rate 3.75% through 2026/27; 10-year PWLB rate 5.72%
findings.quote: when the Council may not be able to avoid new borrowing to finance capital expenditure and/or the refinancing of maturing debt.

findings.paper_title: 7 Annual Treasury Management Review Prudential Indicators 2025-26
findings.headline: Capital expenditure achieved only 51% of budget; £50M rephased to future years without detail on schemes or timescales
findings.detail: Capital spending plan of £103.2M was achieved at only £53M (51% outturn). The paper states this was due to 'rephasing of planned capital expenditure from 2025/26 into future years' but provides no detail on which schemes slipped, why, or when they are now expected to complete. HRA capital £30.7M vs £51.4M budgeted; GF capital £22.3M vs £51.8M budgeted.
findings.matters: A 49% shortfall in capital delivery signals either project delays, funding constraints, or scope reductions. When combined with the council's need to increase external borrowing in future years (as cash buffers deplete), the rephased £50M capital will compete for higher-cost financing. Lenders need visibility of delivery timeline and reason for slippage.
findings.figures: Total capital budget £103.2M; actual £53M; shortfall £50.2M (49%); HRA shortfall £20.7M (40%); GF shortfall £29.5M (57%)
findings.quote: There was rephasing of planned capital expenditure from 2025/26 into future years resulting in an overall reduction in the use of borrowing to finance capital expenditure.

findings.paper_title: 7 Annual Treasury Management Review Prudential Indicators 2025-26
findings.headline: Council borrowed £7.5M specifically to fund additional lending to Swingate LLP joint venture; subsidiary loan portfolio doubled in two years
findings.detail: The General Fund CFR movement of £7M was driven by 'borrowing used to finance additional lending to Swingate LLP as part of the joint venture with Mace'. Swingate loan now stands at £10.262M (repayable 2027/28). Total non-treasury investments in subsidiaries jumped from £14.5M (2024/25) to £23.3M (2025/26), a 60% increase, funded by external PWLB borrowing at 4.31%.
findings.matters: The council is using long-term external borrowing to fund loans to development companies, creating double exposure: if the subsidiaries underperform, the council carries both the capital loss and the debt servicing obligation. The Marshgate loan (£12.972M) is due for repayment in 2026/27, a near-term liquidity event.
findings.figures: Swingate lending £10.262M; Marshgate lending £12.972M; total subsidiary exposure £23.3M; PWLB borrowing for subsidiaries at 4.31% for 5 years
findings.quote: £7.5 Million relating to borrowing used to finance additional lending to Swingate LLP as part of the joint venture with Mace.

findings.paper_title: 7 Annual Treasury Management Review Prudential Indicators 2025-26
findings.headline: Council explicitly flags risk to HRA's 30-year spending plan if interest rates remain at current elevated levels
findings.detail: The HRA carries £273.8M debt with financing costs consuming 12% of net revenue stream. The Risk section states: 'There is a risk to the HRA BP's ability to fund the approved 30-year spending plans if interest rates continue at the current high level, although currently it is anticipated that rates will reduce.' The council expects rates to fall but has identified the HRA as vulnerable if they do not.
findings.matters: The HRA represents 80% of total council debt. The finance team has explicitly identified that sustained high rates pose a material constraint on delivering the 30-year housing business plan. A lender needs to understand this represents a binding constraint on future HRA spending capacity.
findings.figures: HRA CFR £273.8M of total £343.1M; HRA financing costs 12% of net revenue stream vs GF (2)%; total Stevenage debt £266.1M
findings.quote: There is a risk to the HRA BP's ability to fund the approved 30-year spending plans if interest rates continue at the current high level, although currently it is anticipated that rates will reduce.

findings.headline: Build Back audit costs increased £100K due to prior audit qualifications requiring balance sheet remediation back to 2021/22
findings.detail: External audit costs have increased by £100K in 2026/27 to fund a 'build back' exercise proving balances to the last unqualified accounts in 2021/22. This is because 'national issues in the public sector audit market' mean the council's accounts between 2021/22 and now contained qualifications requiring remediation.
findings.matters: Prior audit qualifications and the cost and effort to remediate them signal governance and financial reporting issues material to lender assessment of financial control and reporting quality.
findings.figures: £100K additional external audit costs in 2026/27
findings.quote: The build back (as a result of the national issues in the public sector audit market) requires balances to be proven back to the last set of unqualified accounts 2021/22.

findings.headline: Brent Court housing development (£15.7M) delayed due to continuing gateway approval barriers
findings.detail: The major Brent Court housing scheme remains delayed waiting for HRB gateway 2 approval. The council notes this reflects a wider national issue affecting HRB schemes' ability to obtain statutory approvals, not a council-specific problem.
findings.matters: Major housing capital schemes are core to HRA financial planning and revenue generation. Delays indicate both delivery risk and potential impact on HRA development income and housing supply targets.
findings.figures: £15.7M scheme delayed
findings.quote: Housing Development - £15.7Million – Brent Court - continued delays in receiving gateway 2 approval for the works at the site. This is a national issue whereby schemes considered HRB's are experiencing delays in receiving the necessary statutory approvals to enable works on site.

findings.headline: HRA capital programme reduced by £11M over MTFS period and £20M re-phased from 2026/27, driven by significant financial challenges and high-rise safety works
findings.detail: The HRA capital programme has been substantially re-phased (£20.1M from 2026/27 to future years) and reduced by £11M over the planning period. The council explicitly states this is 'in light of significant financial challenges the HRA faces both from significant savings and the need to fund building high rise safety works that are due to come to the Committee in a later meeting.' This indicates major costs are coming for building safety compliance.
findings.matters: Explicit mention of 'significant financial challenges' driving major capital deferral and reduction is a material indicator of HRA financial stress. High-rise safety works are a regulatory compliance cost that will strain HRA finances.
findings.figures: £20.1M HRA capital re-phased from 2026/27 to future years; £11M reduction over 2026/27 to 2030/31; £5.5M reduction 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.quote: housing investment £4.4Million re-phasing and reduction across 2026/27 to 2028/29 – this has been reprofiled in light of significant financial challenges the HRA faces both from significant savings and the need to fund building high rise safety works that are due to come to the Committee in a later meeting

findings.paper_title: 8 Appendix A - Quarter One 2026-27 Performance Compendium V6
findings.headline: Non-emergency repair completion rate missed target; graffiti clearance at 53% due to vacancies
findings.detail: Non-emergency responsive repairs completed 93.10% within target against a 95% target. Graffiti clearance dropped to 53% vs 80% target, explicitly attributed to "resourcing" and "ongoing vacancies." These signal service capacity constraints.
findings.matters: Service underperformance due to vacancies suggests either unbudgeted recruitment/agency costs to recover performance, or a structural inability to deliver contracted service levels.
findings.figures: Non-emergency repairs 93.10% vs 95% target; Graffiti clearance 53% vs 80% target (8 of 15 reported jobs cleared in June)
findings.quote: Resourcing in June has led to a drop in complete graffiti removal, with eight of the 15 reports being cleared. Performance continues to be affected by ongoing vacancies and the holiday period, with agency staff being used to support service delivery where necessary.

findings.paper_title: 8 Appendix A - Quarter One 2026-27 Performance Compendium V6
findings.headline: Warm Homes retrofit programme running 60% behind plan after Q1
findings.detail: The Warm Homes Local Grant programme, designed to improve energy efficiency for eligible households, shows "progress remains slower than anticipated, with three homes batched for the WHLG during this quarter." This is a three-year programme, suggesting a significant delivery shortfall if the pace does not accelerate.
findings.matters: Underspend on a targeted savings/efficiency programme suggests execution risk or lower-than-expected uptake, affecting both grant drawdown and the council's carbon targets.
findings.figures: 3 homes batched in Q1 of a three-year programme; described as slower than anticipated
findings.quote: Following the promotional activities and feedback sessions with our delivery partner, the National Energy Foundation, progress remains slower than anticipated, with three homes batched for the WHLG during this quarter.

findings.paper_title: 8 Appendix A - Quarter One 2026-27 Performance Compendium V6
findings.headline: Forster Country Park Phase One delayed by site defects; outstanding issues unresolved
findings.detail: The handover of Phase One has been delayed due to "landscaping and planting defects, footpath and drainage works, site maintenance concerns, and finalisation of legal agreements." The council remains in discussions with the developer to ensure standards are met before transfer.
findings.matters: A delayed handover suggests defects in capital delivery or contractor performance, and defers any capital receipt or transfer of maintenance liability.
findings.figures: No financial impact quantified; Phase One still pending handover
findings.quote: The handover of Phase One of the Country Park has been delayed until a number of outstanding issues are resolved, including landscaping and planting defects, footpath and drainage works, site maintenance concerns, and finalisation of legal agreements.

findings.paper_title: 8 Appendix A - Quarter One 2026-27 Performance Compendium V6
findings.headline: Fire safety compliance is lowest-performing area with 13 overdue high-risk actions
findings.detail: Fire compliance is "currently the lowest performing area at 84.11%" with 22 high-risk actions outstanding, of which 13 are overdue. The council has had to explicitly request exemptions from Section 24 Notice requirements for high-rise and building safety works to prevent delays.
findings.matters: Overdue fire safety actions on council-owned stock expose the council to regulatory action, tenant claims, and unbudgeted emergency remediation costs.
findings.figures: 22 high-risk compliance actions outstanding; 13 overdue; Fire compliance 84.11% vs 98.18% for Gas; 501 total remedial actions outstanding of which 159 are overdue
findings.quote: There are currently 22 high-risk actions outstanding, of which 13 are overdue and nine remain in date. The Council continues to focus on reducing overdue and higher-risk remedial actions, particularly within Fire, while maintaining progress across all other compliance areas.

findings.paper_title: 8 Appendix A - Quarter One 2026-27 Performance Compendium V6
findings.headline: Multiple capital housing schemes delayed; Courtlands delayed by UKPN power connectivity failure
findings.detail: Courtlands scheme, which was meant to generate a capital receipt and repay a Marshgate Ltd loan to the council, is delayed due to "faulty equipment" in a UKPN cable diversion. Brent Court demolition is underway but construction will pause pending Gateway Two approval. These delays cascade cash flow and repayment timings.
findings.matters: The Courtlands receipt was intended to repay internal lending; delays to this or other schemes defer repayment and limit the council's capital availability.
findings.figures: One emergency property case could not meet 24-hour Awaab's Law timescale; Brent Court topping-out delayed pending Gateway approval
findings.quote: UKPN works on site were delayed further as a result of faulty equipment which was required for the diversion. This has now been remedied and a new date is anticipated shortly.

findings.paper_title: 8 Appendix A - Quarter One 2026-27 Performance Compendium V6
findings.headline: HRA is financially stressed: substantial savings required for 2027/28
findings.detail: The approved 2026/27 HRA savings programme is being delivered, but the council is now developing a balanced HRA budget for 2027/28 that requires "a substantial level of savings." This signals underlying financial pressure in the housing account and suggests current spending is not sustainable.
findings.matters: An HRA forced to find large savings in the medium term indicates either rising costs (repairs, fire safety remediation) or stagnant income, and narrows the council's financial flexibility.
findings.figures: 2027/28 HRA budget requires "substantial level of savings"; medium-term planning period mentioned but not quantified
findings.quote: Work is also underway to develop a balanced HRA budget for 2027/28 and the medium term, with a comprehensive savings plan being prepared to identify and deliver the substantial level of savings required.

findings.headline: Awaab's Law damp and mould compliance costs £200k pa from 2027/28, new recurring pressure
findings.detail: The council has added £200k annual revenue costs from 2027/28 onwards to meet legal requirements for damp and mould case management under Awaab's Law. This is a new recurring pressure on an already constrained HRA with unresolved savings targets. The cost may be subject to revision as guidance is finalised.
findings.matters: Awaab's Law is a statutory obligation. The council cannot avoid this cost, so it must come from the limited savings pool or reserves. Combined with building safety and other regulatory costs, it narrows the path to HRA balance.
findings.figures: £200k pa from 2027/28 onwards
findings.quote: A further £200K pa has been included from next year to meet the expected costs of meeting the legal requirements of damp and mould case management.

findings.headline: Government rent convergence policy delayed and reduced in scope, limiting income recovery to £700k pa by 2030/31
findings.detail: The Business Plan anticipated rent convergence from April 2026 with a £1 per week cap. Government delayed this to April 2027 and then increased the cap to £2 per week from April 2028. The council notes: 'due to the delayed implementation of the Government's revised rent convergence arrangements, the full benefit of the higher affordability cap will not be realised until 2028/29.' The revised policy is forecast to generate only 'approximately £700K per annum by 2030/31' — less additional income than originally planned. This is a material income shortfall against the Business Plan.
findings.matters: Rent is the HRA's principal income source. A one-year delay in policy implementation and a lower cap than expected reduces income available to service borrowing and meet savings targets. The council was counting on this income to balance the account.
findings.figures: £700k additional annual income by 2030/31 (original plan anticipated higher); convergence starts April 2027 (not April 2026); cap £1 pa first year (April 2027–2028), then £2 pa from April 2028
findings.quote: However, the Government announcement was not made until January 2026 and stated rent convergence would start a year later from April 2027, with a £1 per week cap on increases for the first year, rising to a £2 per week cap from April 2028.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation merger scheduled April 2028, with HRA 'full financial implications still being developed'
findings.detail: Stevenage will merge with North Hertfordshire and Welwyn Hatfield to form a Central Hertfordshire unitary authority in April 2028, combining HRAs with a total of 17,000 homes. The MTFS includes an unspecified allowance for 'transitional costs associated with LGR', but the paper explicitly states 'the full financial implications are still being developed'. The merger may create opportunities for efficiencies but also introduces governance risk and uncertainty during the transition.
findings.matters: Mergers create financial risk: integration costs often exceed estimates, service disruption can occur, and accountability becomes unclear during transition. A lender needs to know the full cost and timeline before the HRA is rebased.
findings.figures: LGR costs: £50k (2026/27), £104k (2027/28), then £0; total housing stock post-merger: 17,000 homes across two HRAs; vesting date: 1 April 2028
findings.quote: The MTFS includes an allowance for transitional costs associated with LGR; however, the full financial implications are still being developed.

findings.headline: PWLB interest rates are 5.01–6.07% against Business Plan assumptions of 4.8–3.80%, creating £567k additional cost per £1m borrowed over 25 years
findings.detail: The Business Plan modelled PWLB rates at 4.8% falling to 3.80% by 2029/30. Current market rates are 5.01% (5-year) and 6.07% (25-year). The council notes: 'for every million borrowed there would be £22,700 more interest, or £567K over a 25-year period.' The HRA benefits from a 0.60% preferential rate from government, but this is only guaranteed until March 2027. The council must refinance £63m of debt within the next five years.
findings.matters: A council refinancing £63m in a higher-rate environment faces materially higher debt service costs. Interest rate risk is the single largest financial exposure in the HRA MTFS. If rates do not fall as assumed, the account will not balance.
findings.figures: Current PWLB rates: 5.01% (5-year), 6.07% (25-year); assumed rates: 4.8% falling to 3.80%; £63m debt to refinance in 5 years; 0.60% preferential discount (guaranteed only to March 2027)
findings.quote: Currently, PWLB rates are higher than the projections used in the Business Plan last year and the HRA still has over £7Million of internal borrowing. The plan assumed a short-term rate of 4.8% falling to 3.80% by 2029/30, but the current rates are 5.01% for a five-year loan and 6.07% for a 25-year loan.

findings.headline: Building safety costs are 'significantly higher than previously forecast' but remain unbudgeted
findings.detail: Specialist surveys of the council's five high-rise residential blocks have identified that building safety works and refurbishment will cost materially more than anticipated. The paper explicitly states: 'no assumptions have yet been included within the MTFS for this future work'. In response, £10m of other capital expenditure has been reprofiled to later years to create flexibility. The final costs are to be 'considered separately by Cabinet in October'. This is a material unknown liability.
findings.matters: High-rise remediation is a statutory obligation under building safety legislation, not discretionary. An unquantified cost liability of this scale creates refinancing risk and may force further savings or borrowing.
findings.figures: £10m of capital expenditure reprofiled to create headroom; no estimate of required building safety spend provided
findings.quote: Specialist consultancy work, updated surveys and wider asset performance reviews have identified that the cost of delivering essential building safety works and wider refurbishment programmes is likely to be significantly higher than previously forecast.

findings.headline: Savings shortfall: £3.6m annual reduction needed but only £959k identified so far
findings.detail: The Business Plan requires £3.6m in recurring annual revenue savings over the next four years to maintain a balanced HRA. Service directors have identified £1.5m of potential savings 'being reviewed', leaving approximately £1.1m unresolved. The paper states these must be delivered 'in order to stay in line with the Business Plan projections' but reserves that savings will be brought forward through future budget-setting cycles. The CFO notes this is 'critical' to achieving balance.
findings.matters: An HRA with an unresolved multi-million-pound structural deficit is a credit risk. The council will need to either cut services or use reserves to plug the gap if savings are not found.
findings.figures: £3.6m pa required over 4 years; £459k identified 2026/27, rising to £959k 2027/28–2029/30; £1.5m 'being reviewed'
findings.quote: This graph shows that current revenue spend will need to fall by £3.6Million per annum over the next four years, in order to stay in line with the Business Plan projections.

The council attributes some misses to tenant scheduling and access delays, but this remains a regulatory failure that could trigger Housing Ombudsman or regulator enforcement.
findings.matters: This is a specific breach of a statutory housing safety requirement; continued non-compliance risks enforcement action, reputation damage, and potential fines or intervention.

findings.detail: The leisure club capital program (KE566) rises from £5.79m (Q4) to £7.10m (Q1) in 2026/27 (+£1.31m). However, 2027/28 is then revised down by £2.2m from £24.1m to £21.9m forecast. findings.matters: Large regeneration schemes are execution-dependent and market-dependent. Material revisions to spending profile within a single quarter signal either unknown project risks or changing market appetite for the work.

findings.detail: The Oval regeneration project has experienced site delays 'primarily relating to delays from Statutory Utility providers in diverting existing services'. This major project has £2.5M rephased from 2025/26 to 2026/27 due to these external dependencies, indicating the council has limited control over delivery timescales on a key regeneration initiative.
findings.matters: Capital programme delivery risk is driven by external parties (utility providers) outside council control; major regeneration spend faces timing slippage.

findings.headline: The council has 45 open housing disrepair compensation cases with potential for 40 additional cases in 2026/27
findings.detail: After reviewing open cases, the council carried forward £222.5K to cover likely disrepair compensation costs. Current open cases include 10 from 2025/26, with 'the potential for another 40 cases in this year'. Last year ~60 cases were closed, but the council can only 'target' ending 2026/27 with 25 open cases, indicating the rate of new complaints exceeds closures.
findings.matters: Significant and growing service complaint/compensation liability; suggests housing maintenance backlog and potential statutory compliance issues with housing conditions.
findings.figures: 45 open cases currently; potential for 40 additional in 2026/27; £222.5K carry forward; target 25 closed cases by end 2026/27

findings.headline: The HRA wrote off £800K of uncollectable housing rent arrears in Q4 2025/26
findings.detail: Following a major debt review, the council wrote off £800K as irrecoverable. Total rent arrears stand at £3.0M at year-end but are only covered by a £1.8M provision (61% coverage). The council identifies 'ongoing pressure relating to the universal credit which increases the challenge of rent collection' as a persistent factor.
findings.matters: Material bad debt write-off indicates collection weakness; only 61% provision against arrears suggests future write-offs likely; universal credit pressures are structural, not cyclical.
findings.figures: £800K write-off; £3.0M arrears; £1.8M provision (61% coverage)
findings.quote: After a major review of HRA debt an £800K write off was made in the last quarter of 2025/26... Total arrears for the HRA at the end of 2025/26 stood at £3.0 Million and are covered by a provision of £1.8 Million (61% coverage)... There is also ongoing pressure relating to the universal credit which increases the challenge of rent collection.

findings.headline: The council's wholly owned company Marshgate failed to repay its scheduled loan in 2025/26
findings.detail: Marshgate (the WOC) did not repay its loan to the council as scheduled, forcing the council to make a £223K MRP charge. The repayment is now 'scheduled for 2026/27'. This signals a cash flow issue in the subsidiary and means the parent council cannot rely on forecast loan repayments from its own company.
findings.matters: Subsidiary debt default raises questions about WOC cash flow and financial sustainability; parent council is exposed to repayment timing risk on its own subsidiary.
findings.figures: £223K MRP charge required; loan repayment deferred from 2025/26 to 2026/27
findings.quote: the Council's Wholly Owned Company (WOC), Marshgate, did not repay its loan to the Council in 2025/26 but is scheduled now for 2026/27... As the loan remained outstanding at the year end, the Council was required to make an MRP charge in accordance with the regulations.

findings.headline: Supported housing provision creates an ongoing structural funding gap that Housing Benefit does not fully reimburse
findings.detail: The council overspent by £416K in 2025/26 on housing benefit due to a rise in supported housing provision. The council states this 'is part of a national trend affecting many Local Authorities' but notes that while 'Housing Benefit covers the accommodation provision, it does not fully reimburse the Council for the supported accommodation element, resulting in a funding gap'. Officers are monitoring but flagging the impact for the MTFS.
findings.matters: This is a structural deficit on a statutory service with no apparent funding solution; it will recur annually and compounds the GF budget pressure.
findings.figures: £416K overspend in 2025/26
findings.quote: While Housing Benefit covers the accommodation provision, it does not fully reimburse the Council for the supported accommodation element, resulting in a funding gap. Officers are monitoring the position closely on a monthly basis to assess what the ongoing financial impact and any implications for future budgets will be included in the Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS).

findings.headline: The HRA Business Plan requires significant year-on-year savings for four years to balance the account
findings.detail: Despite a £1.5M surplus in 2025/26, the medium and long-term forecasts indicate increasing cost pressures. The council faces 'increased regulation and operating requirements, coinciding with higher borrowing costs' that 'have significantly increased financial risk'. Work to develop savings options has already begun for the 2027/28 budget, and the council warns that 'overall balances are set to reduce in coming years'.
findings.matters: A core service (housing) faces structural deficit requiring deep cuts over the medium term; indicates significant financial stress ahead despite the current year's positive outturn.
findings.figures: £1,543,209 in-year HRA surplus but 'significant year on year savings for the next four years' required; HRA balance projected to reduce from £12.5M
findings.quote: Despite the larger than anticipated surplus in the HRA for 2025/26, the medium and longer term forecasts continue to indicate increasing cost pressures... increased regulation and operating requirements, coinciding with higher borrowing costs, have significantly increased financial risk... identified the need to make significant year on year savings for the next four years in order to balance the account.

The specific issues are recorded in the Annual Governance Statement and will be monitored by the Corporate Governance Group.
findings.matters: An audit opinion below full assurance indicates identified control weaknesses and non-compliance, relevant to lenders assessing governance quality and the council's financial control environment.

findings.headline: Historic MRP overpayment of £1,057,660.39 reduces regeneration asset MRP charges through 2025/26
findings.detail: Following a 2019/20 review of asset lives, the council identified that MRP had been overpaid historically. Under MHCLG guidance this overpayment can be reclaimed. As a result, no MRP is charged for regeneration assets until 2025/26, when the remaining balance (£89,144.79) will be used, after which full MRP charges resume.
findings.matters: Reduces the council's MRP budget requirement for 2025/26 but signals that 2026/27 will see a step-up in MRP charges for regeneration assets as the overpayment is exhausted

findings.headline: Technology cost savings of £40k in 2028-29 are conditional on unproven proof-of-concept outcomes
findings.detail: M365 migration is proposed as a cost saving option, but delivery is explicitly contingent: 'Depending on the outcome of a proof of the concepts over the next nine months, replacing the virtual desktop solution with M365 will result in further savings of £40k in 2028/29.' The proposal includes zero savings in Years 1 and 2, meaning the benefit is speculative and delayed 2-3 years.
findings.matters: Budget planning should rely on confirmed savings, not conditional ones. If the proof of concept fails or reveals higher implementation costs, the £40k saving will not materialize and the council will need an alternative.

findings.headline: Waste charging income is included in budget options but will not materialize until 2027-28, creating timing misalignment
findings.detail: Stevenage proposes charging new developments for waste and recycling receptacles, with the council seeking approval in 2026-27 to begin issuing charging packs to developers. However, the proposal explicitly states: 'the projected additional income from bin deliveries will not materialise until 2027/28 onwards.' This means anticipated income of £8,100 in Year 2 (2027-28) is being included in near-term budget proposals despite not arriving for 12-18 months.
findings.matters: Including income in budget options that won't materialize until the following financial year creates a timing gap - if the income is being relied upon to balance the 2026-27 budget as proposed, there is a hole that must be filled by other means.

findings.quote: Although the projected additional income from bin deliveries will not materialise until 2027/28 onwards, approval is sought at this stage to enable officers to begin issuing charging packs to external developers from this financial year (2025/26).

findings.headline: Customer Services management role deletion relies on existing temporary arrangements rather than permanent replacement
findings.detail: A permanent management role in Customer Services is proposed for deletion, to be covered by 'temporary arrangements currently in place' rather than a permanent replacement. This approach saves £12,150 in Year 1 rising to £16,200 in Year 2, but substitutes temporary staffing for permanent management capacity in a customer-facing service.
findings.matters: Using temporary arrangements to cover a permanently deleted management role raises questions about service continuity and may indicate budget constraints preventing permanent investment, signalling potential staffing instability.
findings.quote: A management saving is proposed within the Customer Service Centre through the deletion of one management role. No redundancies are expected, as temporary arrangements are currently in place.

findings.headline: £5.5m Oval development borrowing creates £137.5k annual revenue cost starting 2029/30, committing future budgets.
findings.detail: The council is borrowing £5.5m over 2027/28 and 2028/29 to fund community and retail assets at the Oval. This will create an annual minimum revenue provision (debt repayment) cost of £137.5k starting in 2029/30. This new revenue commitment reduces financial flexibility and must be accommodated in future General Fund budgets alongside other pressures.
findings.matters: Lenders assess total debt servicing costs and their impact on revenue budget. New fixed revenue commitments reduce the council's ability to manage budget pressures and increase the risk of service cuts or further borrowing if revenues decline.
findings.figures: £5.5m borrowing for Oval 2027/28–2028/29; £137.5k annual MRP from 2029/30 onwards
findings.quote: The indicative annual revenue costs of the scheme include £137.5k MRP for repayment of the principal commencing in 2029/30 in the General Fund budget.

findings.headline: Current asset maintenance approach will lead to building closures if capital funding is not sustained.
findings.detail: The council operates a 'fix on fail' maintenance approach to assets due to limited capital funding. The strategy document explicitly states this "cannot be sustained in the medium to long term" as it will cause "gradual degradation" and "inevitably lead to close of buildings". The council is also at risk of non-compliance with Energy Performance Certificate requirements and climate change obligations, creating potential legal liability.
findings.matters: Deteriorating asset condition creates future emergency capital expenditure risk and potential service disruptions. Legal compliance failures expose the council to enforcement action and additional unplanned costs.
findings.figures: No specific figures; described as inevitable outcome of continued underfunding.
findings.quote: This approach cannot be sustained in the medium to long term as it will lead to a gradual degradation of the Council's assets with reactive works only being undertaken to keep sites wind and watertight.

findings.headline: Capital investment need of £127m exceeds achievable receipts of £44m, leaving £83m structural gap.
findings.detail: The council identified capital investment needs of £127m but assesses that only £44m of capital receipts can be realised. Even if all approved receipts are delivered, the document states there will be "a requirement to find alternative funding strategies or third-party funding to meet the gap". This indicates the council's capital plans depend on external funding beyond its own resources.
findings.matters: An £83m structural funding gap signals that the council may face difficult trade-offs between capital investment, service viability and borrowing levels, or may become dependent on third-party funding or asset disposals outside its control.
findings.figures: Capital investment need £127m; achievable capital receipts £44m; structural gap £83m
findings.quote: The high-level assessment in the November 2023 report of the potential value of capital receipts that could be realised by SBC is £44Million which is significantly less than the cost of investment needed of £127Million.

findings.headline: 2026/27 capital receipts forecast cut by £5.9m, reducing funding available and requiring early borrowing.
findings.detail: The council has substantially revised its 2026/27 capital receipts forecast downward from £9.5m to £3.6m. This forecast volatility reflects delayed Kenilworth disposals and lower garage sale proceeds (only £200k expected in 2027/28 versus the original £700k forecast). The council has responded by bringing forward planned borrowing of £3.2m to 2026/27, increasing borrowing costs.
findings.matters: Lenders need reliable capital receipt forecasts to evaluate debt capacity and receipt-backed repayment plans. Large forecast revisions suggest property market weakness or disposal delays that create refinancing risk.
findings.figures: 2026/27 receipts down £5.9m (from £9.5m to £3.6m); garage sales revised from £1.35m to £1.1m; timing shift: only £200k expected 2027/28 vs £700k planned
findings.quote: Garage sales of £1.35Million forecast to be received from 2027/28 to 2028-29 have been revised down to £1.1Million with only £200k expected in 2027/28 rather than the original £700k forecast when the Garage improvement programme was approved.

findings.headline: £16m short-term borrowing scheduled for 2027/28 repayment is at risk from delayed capital receipts.
findings.detail: The council has taken £16m in short-term borrowing for SG1 regeneration, garage improvements and housing schemes, planned to be repaid by 2027/28 from capital receipts. However, major receipt forecasts have slipped—Kenilworth phase II (£6m) moved from 2026/27 to 2027/28, and garage sales cut 18.5%—creating liquidity risk if receipts don't materialise as planned.
findings.matters: A lender needs predictability around when short-term borrowing will be repaid. Delays to receipt realisation increase the risk of failed repayment or need for refinancing.
findings.figures: £16m short-term borrowing due 2027/28; £6m Kenilworth slippage; garage sales revised from £1.35m to £1.1m
findings.quote: The total borrowing recommended of £32Million includes £16Million of short term borrowing for SG1 Joint Venture, garage improvements, and Housing Development schemes the latter scheduled to be repaid by 2027/28 using capital receipts profiled to be received by that year.

findings.paper_title: 01 final Council tax and General Fund report 2026-27 COUNCIL
findings.headline: Savings plan for 2027/28–2029/30 depends entirely on annual fees and charges increases; £800k target with no identified service reductions.
findings.detail: The November 2025 Balancing the Budget report identified a shortfall of £1.15m for 2027/28–2029/30. This has been reduced to £800k, and the council now proposes to meet it entirely through annual fees and charges increases with no further savings required. The sustainability of this approach depends on fees income not being eroded by demand shifts or economic conditions. No service cuts are built into the savings plan.
findings.matters: Lenders assess the robustness of savings plans. A plan with no service reductions and full reliance on income growth from fees is vulnerable to recessionary conditions or demand suppression. The paper flags medium risk that 'fees and charges income' may fall short in a difficult economic climate.
